paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Sampling bias is a flaw in the way a sample is gathered. Some members of the population a study means to describe end up with a better or worse chance of being picked than others. The sample that results is called biased, because not every individual was equally likely to land in it.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The danger is a wrong conclusion. If nobody corrects for the bias, a result can be credited to the thing under study when it really comes from how the sample was drawn. One view, not shared by everyone, says sampling bias harms external validity: how well the findings carry over to the whole population.

paragraphs.heading: Other names
paragraphs.text: In medicine the same problem is sometimes called ascertainment bias. Sampling bias is usually counted as one kind of selection bias, though some people keep the two apart. In practice the two names are often swapped freely.

paragraphs.heading: Leaving groups out
paragraphs.text: One form comes from drawing the sample in one particular place. A survey of teenage drug use handed out in high schools misses teens who are home-schooled or have dropped out. A street interview that stops passers-by catches too many healthy people and too few with a chronic illness, who are less often out of the house. When a group is shut out entirely, its members have zero chance of selection, which may be an extreme form of the problem.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing yourself
paragraphs.text: Self-selection bias can arise whenever the people being studied decide for themselves whether to take part. That choice may be tied to traits that affect the study, so those who join are not typical. People with strong opinions or deep knowledge are keener to spend time on a survey. So online and phone-in polls overrepresent the highly motivated, hear less from the indifferent, and give extreme views too much weight. For this reason such polls are regarded as unscientific.

paragraphs.heading: Survivors and hospitals
paragraphs.text: Survivorship bias looks only at what survived and ignores what dropped out of view. Judging the economy by the firms that exist today, for instance, leaves out every business that failed. Berkson's fallacy is the hospital version: a study population drawn from patients is less healthy than people in general. This can produce a false negative link between diseases, since a patient without diabetes is more likely to have some other illness, such as cholecystitis, that brought them in.
